name: netstat
title: Understanding netstat
summary: Displays active TCP/UDP connections, listening ports, routing table, interface statistics, and per-protocol statistics to help diagnose network and port usage on Windows.

examples.description: Lists all connections and listening ports with numeric addresses and the owning process ID (PID). Useful to identify which PID has a port open.
Filters numeric output to show connections/listeners on TCP/UDP port 80. Helpful for confirming HTTP port usage or conflicts.
Shows all connections/listeners with the executable (-b), numeric addresses (-n), and PID (-o). Requires elevation; useful for mapping ports directly to binaries.
Displays the IP routing table (same as route print). Use this to verify default gateways and route precedence.
Shows TCP protocol statistics only. Useful for spotting retransmissions, resets, and overall TCP health.
Displays all connections and listening ports and attempts to resolve foreign addresses to FQDNs. Helpful when you need human-readable remote endpoints.

permissions.notes: Most netstat output is available to standard users. Options like -b (executable mapping) often require an elevated Command Prompt. Some entries may show 'Can not obtain ownership information' without admin rights or if the process exits quickly.

risk.warning: Read-only command; however, it may reveal sensitive process names, IPs, and ports in logs or screenshots. Use -n to avoid unnecessary DNS lookups on production systems.

output_fields.name: -a
output_fields.description: Shows all connections and listening ports. Essential when verifying whether a service is actually listening.

output_fields.name: -n
output_fields.description: Disables DNS/FQDN lookups and shows numeric addresses. Avoids delays and makes scripting/filtering predictable.

output_fields.name: -o
output_fields.description: Displays the owning process ID. Critical for correlating ports to processes for remediation.

output_fields.name: -b
output_fields.description: Displays the executable creating each connection or listener. Often requires elevation; invaluable for identifying the exact binary.

output_fields.name: -p Proto
output_fields.description: Filters by protocol (TCP, UDP, TCPv6, UDPv6, IP, IPv6, ICMP, ICMPv6). Reduces noise and focuses analysis.

output_fields.name: Proto
output_fields.description: Output column indicating protocol (TCP or UDP). Helps separate connection-oriented vs connectionless traffic.

output_fields.name: Local Address
output_fields.description: IP and port bound locally (0.0.0.0 or [::] means all interfaces). Key for exposure/scope of a listening service.

output_fields.name: Foreign Address
output_fields.description: Remote endpoint IP/port. Identifies who you are connected to or receiving from.

output_fields.name: State
output_fields.description: TCP connection state (LISTENING, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT, etc.). Indicates lifecycle/health of connections.

output_fields.name: PID
output_fields.description: Owning process identifier (with -o). Needed to map ports to processes via tasklist or Task Manager.

output_fields.name: -r
output_fields.description: Shows the routing table. Useful for validating default route and specific network paths.

output_fields.name: -s
output_fields.description: Displays per-protocol statistics. Helps quantify errors, resets, and packet counts.

output_fields.name: -t
output_fields.description: Shows TCP offload state. Useful when troubleshooting NIC offload/acceleration issues.

output_fields.name: -q
output_fields.description: Displays all connections, listening ports, and bound non-listening TCP ports. Helps spot sockets in a bound state without a listener.

common_errors.meaning: Occurs when using options like -b (show executable) without an elevated Command Prompt. Run as Administrator.
Seen with netstat -b when the tool cannot map a socket to an executable (insufficient rights or the process exited). Try elevation and rerun promptly.
Name resolution delays when not using -n or when using -f to resolve FQDNs. Use -n to disable lookups or ensure DNS is responsive.
Using an unsupported protocol token (e.g., netstat -p foo). Use one of: TCP, UDP, TCPv6, UDPv6, IP, IPv6, ICMP, ICMPv6.
Normal condition when there are no current TCP sessions. Verify service is listening (-a) or traffic is present.

common_errors.message: 'netstat' is not recognized as an internal or external command...
common_errors.meaning: PATH/environment issue or severely minimal Windows environment. Ensure %SystemRoot%\System32 is in PATH and the binary exists.
